question: What shape is an intrauterine device (IUD)?
explanation: IUDs are built with a small frame shaped like the letter T so they fit comfortably inside the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h1)

question: Why is an IUD called a long-acting reversible contraceptive?

options.A: It only prevents pregnancy for a maximum of three months
options.B: It is permanent and cannot be taken out once inserted
options.C: It requires taking daily pills to stay effective
options.D: It protects against pregnancy for years, but fertility returns after removal

explanation: You get years of steady protection, but if the client ever wants to get pregnant later, you just take it out and her natural fertility bounces right back! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h1)

question: How does a copper IUD mainly prevent pregnancy?

options.A: By releasing high doses of estrogen to stop ovulation
options.B: By swelling the cervix shut so sperm cannot enter
options.C: By physically blocking the Fallopian tubes with wire
options.D: By releasing copper ions that stun and damage sperm cells

explanation: The copper creates an environment that sperm really hate. It damages them and stops them from ever reaching the egg! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h2)

question: How does a hormonal IUD prevent pregnancy?

options.A: By thickening the cervical mucus to block sperm from entering
options.B: By making the vagina super acidic to destroy sperm on contact
options.C: By tricking the ovaries into releasing multiple eggs
options.D: By creating physical pressure that crushes any fertilized egg

explanation: The tiny bit of hormone released thickens the mucus at the cervix like a strong security guard—sperm just can't swim through it! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h2)

question: How long can the common Copper T 380A IUD stay in place?

options.A: For the rest of the woman's life

explanation: The Copper T 380A is a real champion for long-term family planning—it's approved to stay in safely for up to a decade! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h3)

question: A client complains of heavy, painful periods and wants an IUD. Which type should you recommend to help with the heavy bleeding?

options.A: A hormonal IUD that releases levonorgestrel
options.C: Any IUD, because all types stop bleeding completely
options.D: A plain plastic loop with no hormones or metal

explanation: Hormonal IUDs are great because they lighten the uterine lining over time, which usually means much lighter, less painful periods for the client. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h3)

question: Which of these is a strict 'no-go' (absolute contraindication) for putting in an IUD?

options.B: Having had a past cesarean section
options.C: A history of high blood pressure

explanation: Never place an IUD if a woman is already pregnant! It can cause serious complications, severe infection, or miscarriage. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h4)

question: Why must you perform a bimanual pelvic exam before putting in an IUD?

options.A: To confirm the client is definitely not ovulating
options.B: To stretch the cervix open without using instruments
options.C: To check the weight of the client's ovaries
options.D: To check the size and position of the uterus

explanation: Feeling the uterus first helps you know its exact angle and size so you can insert the device safely without accidentally poking through the uterine wall. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h4)

question: Which sterile instrument is used to gently hold and steady the cervix during an IUD procedure?
explanation: The tenaculum gently holds the cervix steady and straightens out the angle of the uterus so you can pass the IUD smoothly. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h5)

question: What is the main reason for using a uterine sound before IUD insertion?

options.A: To numb the inside of the uterus against cramps
options.B: To measure how deep and in which direction the uterus goes
options.C: To clean out blood and mucus from the canal
options.D: To widen the vagina so the speculum opens wider

explanation: Sounding gives you an exact measurement of the uterine depth, making sure you don't push the IUD in too far and cause a perforation. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h5)

question: What important advice should you give a client about her IUD strings?

options.A: Come to the clinic weekly for string trimming
options.B: Pull gently on the strings every morning to check if it's tight
options.C: Cut the strings shorter with scissors if they curl up
options.D: Check for the strings inside the vagina after every monthly period

explanation: Teach clients to do a quick finger check for their strings after their period to make sure the IUD is still sitting snugly in place. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h6)

question: A client who just got a copper IUD a month ago complains of slightly heavier periods and mild cramps. What is your best response as her nurse?

options.A: Tell her she has a dangerous infection that needs surgery
options.B: Schedule emergency surgery to close her cervix
options.C: Tell her to take it out herself at home right away
options.D: Reassure her that this is normal at first and discuss pain relief

explanation: Copper IUDs often cause heavier periods and mild cramping during the first few weeks or months. Reassure your patient—it usually settles down! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h6)

question: When is the risk of getting pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) highest after an IUD insertion?

options.A: Only if the client gets pregnant with the IUD
options.B: During the first 20 days after insertion
options.C: There is never any risk of infection
options.D: After the IUD has been in place for five years

explanation: Because tiny amounts of bacteria can accidentally enter the uterus during the procedure, the infection risk is highest right after insertion, during the first few weeks. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h7)

question: A client comes back to the clinic three weeks after getting an IUD with severe lower belly pain, fever, and strange vaginal discharge. What should you suspect first?

options.A: The IUD completely falling out on its own
options.C: A normal adjustment period to the device

explanation: Fever, foul discharge, and severe lower abdominal pain are classic red flags for an ascending uterine infection like PID. Act fast and evaluate her! [learn more](GNS226_U6_T015#GNS226_U6_T015_h7)
